description: We are APS from Maputo, Mozambique - Final Year Web Programming students. Ours skills involve: Web Development, JavaScript, React, UI/UX, DB Management, PHP, Python, Java and many more. We build solutions for real life problems. Join us to learn, create, and build a portfolio-ready NASA project. Looking for designers, data & storytelling members.
summary:
Little Astronauts is a junior astronaut mission trainer: a web game where young players learn how astronauts make safe decisions on a Moon or Mars mission. Trainees prepare on Earth by choosing a destination and loading cargo, then travel and work on the surface. Along the way, they face incidents such as equipment problems and must decide how to respond. Each choice is safe, risky, or recoverable, and a final debrief provides a score out of 100 and up to three stars, with the reason for each result.
It addresses the challenge by turning real mission practice into training that children can try. Each mission is based on a real spacewalk from NASA’s Extra-vehicular Activity (EVA) dataset for the United States and Russia, and the kind of work done on that spacewalk, such as repair or science, shapes the first incident on the surface.
It matters because few young people ever see the decisions behind space exploration. Practising them safely in a game builds careful thinking and interest in science and engineering.
details:
What it does and how it works
Little Astronauts is a game where kids train for a Moon or Mars mission. You pick where to go, pack water, food, oxygen and fuel (the ship can only carry so much), fly there, land, and start working. Then things go wrong, as they do in real missions: power drops, radiation rises, a rover gets stuck. At each problem you choose what to do. One choice is safe, one is risky, and sometimes there’s a way to recover. At the end you get a score out of 100, up to three stars, and a simple explanation of why each problem happened. On the surface you can also step outside in an EVA suit, but the oxygen tank only lasts five minutes, so you have to move fast and smart.

Each mission starts from a real spacewalk. We used NASA’s public record of 371 American and Russian spacewalks from 1965 to 2013. The game shows who went out, in which spacecraft, when, for how long and why. The kind of work they did, like a repair or an installation, decides one of the problems you’ll meet on the surface. When the mission ends, you can compare your time with the real one.

Benefits
Kids get to practise space decisions without any equipment, and they find out why a choice was good or bad instead of just being told. It works in Portuguese and English, and once the NASA data is saved it keeps working without internet.

Intended impact
We want kids to get curious about space and to learn that careful thinking matters more than speed.

Tools we used
The server is written in Python with FastAPI and PostgreSQL. The game itself is JavaScript with Phaser 3, and everything you see on screen is drawn in code, so there are no image files. NumPy runs a small neural network, and an optional local model (Llama 3.2 through Ollama) helps the game understand typed answers. We wrote automated tests for the mission rules and the NASA data. Everything was built on ordinary Windows laptops. We also used Claude (Anthropic) for parts of the code, tests, slides and writing, and the team reviewed and tested everything.

How it’s creative
The three crew members (command, engineering and operations) react to how the mission is going. Their reactions come from a tiny neural network, but their words are always pre-written, so a child never hears anything unexpected. Players learn from consequences, not quizzes, and every mission is tied to something that really happened in orbit. Teams can also play the same mission together.

What we considered
Safety was the first thing. Players use nicknames, younger players need a guardian’s approval, crew chat uses preset phrases, contact details and links are filtered, you can block other players, and chat messages are deleted after a week. We also made sure the game never calls the internet while someone is playing, so a slow connection can’t ruin a mission. For accuracy, the Moon and Mars trip times come from Apollo 11 and Perseverance, and the game openly says it simplifies some things.
